pr_title: Linting: Update linter to enforce ES 2018 features
pr_body:
Fixed #25185.

**Description**

Update linter to enforce ES 2018 features.

This has four changes:
- add setting to configure linter to enforce 2018 features
- separate config for linting into config file.
- update the 3 header imports that were using 2020 features
- to maintain the same public interface, add export objects MathUtils, AnimationUtils, and DataUtils

The setting that does the work of enforcing 2018 features is:

```json
  "parserOptions": {
    "ecmaVersion": 2018,
    "sourceType": "module"
  },
```

The 'module' setting has been provided by the custom style plugin, it is duplicated here for clarity.  This also ensures that the style plugin is only providing styles rules.

This also overrides the environment setting from the custom plugin to ensure only 2018 globals are defined.  Browser and node settings are duplicated for clarity.  This also ensures that the style plugin is only providing styles rules.

```json
  "env": {
    "browser": true,
    "node": true,
    "es2018": true
  },
```


The lines in 'Three.js' using 2020 syntax were:

```js
export * as AnimationUtils from './animation/AnimationUtils.js';
export * as MathUtils from './math/MathUtils.js';
export * as DataUtils from './extras/DataUtils.js';
```

With an export object added, these become:

```js
export { AnimationUtils } from './animation/AnimationUtils.js';
export { MathUtils } from './math/MathUtils.js';
export { DataUtils } from './extras/DataUtils.js';
```

If the project wants to remove a dependency, we can copy the 15 lines of style settings from the plugin into the lint config file.
pr_comments: MathUtils, AnimationUtils, and DataUtils need to be updated to export their namespaces.
If the project wants to remove a dependency, copy the 15 lines of style settings into the lint config file.

Anyone worried about tree-shaking:

As a confirmation take a look at what we ship now using the 2020 syntax.  I'm going to use the middle size one as an example to reduce the reading.

The old 2020 line:

```js
export * as AnimationUtils from './animation/AnimationUtils.js';
```

Is currently being translated to:

```js
var AnimationUtils = /*#__PURE__*/Object.freeze({
	__proto__: null,
	arraySlice: arraySlice,
	convertArray: convertArray,
	flattenJSON: flattenJSON,
	getKeyframeOrder: getKeyframeOrder,
	isTypedArray: isTypedArray,
	makeClipAdditive: makeClipAdditive,
	sortedArray: sortedArray,
	subclip: subclip
});
```

This has been updated to:

```js
const AnimationUtils = {
	arraySlice: arraySlice,
	convertArray: convertArray,
	isTypedArray: isTypedArray,
	getKeyframeOrder: getKeyframeOrder,
	sortedArray: sortedArray,
	flattenJSON: flattenJSON,
	subclip: subclip,
	makeClipAdditive: makeClipAdditive
};
```

It gets translated to:

```js
const AnimationUtils = {
	arraySlice: arraySlice,
	convertArray: convertArray,
	isTypedArray: isTypedArray,
	getKeyframeOrder: getKeyframeOrder,
	sortedArray: sortedArray,
	flattenJSON: flattenJSON,
	subclip: subclip,
	makeClipAdditive: makeClipAdditive
};
```

Keeping it clean, the final bundler (client application) works its magics.  Its possible we get slightly better tree-shake using the 2018 syntax.  Keep in mind this is an isolated context, relating to a library (not client application), and a very specific import command.

In the old code, final bundler can only remove the whole object if its entirely unused, which will be created in any case (new or old code).  Tools can remove constants if they are entirely unused, so we have even ground.

For evaluation, a test rig of the different builds and tree shake effects can be found here:

https://github.com/epreston/three-treeshake-coverage

Comment and uncomment the different imports, build and inspect the results in the dist folder.

In all cases, `AnimationUtils` is correctly tree-shaken.

Is it possible to configure the linter to enforce ES2018 features, but to ignore ES2020 import/export syntax? I don't think there is any problem with shipping those ES2020 exports, and might allow us to make a narrower change here.

If that's not possible, that's OK, but I didn't see that mentioned in the thread so far.

Anything's possible with configuration and tooling.  We have great ideas for partial solutions going 2020 with restrictions.  I don't see a built in way to approach the problem from that direction (2018 with 2020 imports).

In all cases, we never ship these exports.  The code this replaces is a developer convenience to shave 20 lines off the code we maintain.  The code it generates is equal.  What we trade is complexity, validation of PRs, and standards with partial solutions.
I see – thanks! No concerns about the exports in that case, changing them to reflect how they already get shipped in the bundle sounds good.

Yes this PR does not affect tree-shaking, nor does it make it better.

My point is that this PR changes the exports in a confusing way for no apparent reason, since the import/exports get compiled away. I don't see how this change is beneficial for future maintainers to understand what is going on. The real issue is with eslint, a tool shouldn't dictate how we structure our code.

But I guess this can be overlooked one since it's supposed to be temporary.

We want to have automated warnings when our source code is not ES2018 compliant. I would've ideally excluded imports/exports from that, since they're handled by the build process anyway, but that path doesn't seem to be practical, so I'm fine with changing the imports/exports this way for now. We can clean them up later if needed.

It's not just about 1-2 unsupported ES2020 features — we want our code to be ES2018 compliant, and we don't want to be surprised by a bit of newer syntax sneaking in, or surprised by transpilers doing something we didn't expect. I worry that just enforcing ES2020 and adding custom rules on top will not give us those guarantees, is that wrong?

I'm confused.  Changing the only 3 imports that are using a different syntax so they are the same as other 100 adds confusion ?  The lines that created confusion about tree-shaking ?

The project agrees on a syntax level, they is set in one line, PR's get validated against it, no gaps.  You set any tool to 2018 and you get the same results.  Seems kinda clean having it configured according to the manual in the most typical way.

> we don't want to be surprised by a bit of newer syntax sneaking in

Please don't look at line 1891 of `examples/GLTFExporter.js` until I submit a PR.
Hmm yeah I guess there is no way of having full ES2018 coverage without changing the import as well.
@mrdoob can we wrap this up ?  I'd like to move on to the next.

issue_context.title: Update linter to enforce ES features
issue_context.body:
### Description

We'll want to update the linter (#23763) to ensure that ES2018 syntax is used consistently in both source and addons (see #25172). Currently it accepts a browserslist rather than an ES version to ensure that experimental browser APIs are used responsibly. This doesn't replace discussion around the use of those features, though.

### Solution

I'd like to replace or add on (preference for the first) a linter plugin that checks against ES features only. This is a common enough thing for me to be comfortable writing one on top of a parser if we can't find something well supported. As this widely affects quality control, this should have great language testing coverage before running wild here.

### Alternatives

Transpilation was mentioned in #24237, but discarded in favor of lighter to no tooling. I'll want to echo that in choice of linter tooling around this issue.

### Additional context

I haven't considered updating browerslist as per https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/issues/121#issuecomment-646956379 since that would give false positives for browser APIs. As this is a moving target, I don't think it's appropriate to update mdcs.
comments:
I have a few questions:

The goal is to enforce 2018 syntax across all source and examples ?

The plugin `eslint-config-mdcs` enforces 2020 syntax for the last 3 years, does that align ?  Is it still maintained, will you keep the dependency ?  The rules can be copied over if you want to keep the functionality but drop the dependency.

A few observations:

I didn't find an `ecmaVersion` defined in the `eslintConfig` section of the `package.json`.  Ommitting the other settings for clarity, it should look like:

```json
  "eslintConfig": {
    "parserOptions": {
      "ecmaVersion": 2018
    },
  },
```

If you set eslint to 2018, it correctly errors on line 89 of `Three.js`, because it is 2020 syntax as shown below.

```js
export * as AnimationUtils from './animation/AnimationUtils.js';
```

Some options:

- Set `ecmaVersion` to 2020 and be done with it.  It's 2023, existing tools are enforcing 2020, code has 2020 features, 'optional chaining' could simplify lots of the code base (see below).  If the project has been shipping this without complaints, you might be in safe territory.  

- ecmaVersion version to 2018 and update `Three.js` explicitly export `AnimationUtils` classes.

What are your thoughts ?  We can make lots of progress on this with a very little code.


Optional Chaining: (Taken from Wikipedia)

Optional chaining makes it possible to access the nested properties of an object without having an AND check at each level. An example is `const zipcode = person?.address?.zipcode`. If any of the properties are not present, `zipcode` will be `undefined`.

I think the idea is that the build process will compile the _imports and exports_ appropriately — there's only one file in the bundle at the end of the day, that's Rollup's job. The rest of the codebase, excluding imports and exports, should use ES2018. Is that an option we can configure ESLint for?

My general feeling is that we don't really need features like nullish coalescing right now, the DX improvement isn't meaningful at this time, and some tools have broken when these features have gone into the build accidentally. We just want to prevent that from happening again — using ES2020 is a non-goal for now.

@donmccurdy yes, just add the setting above to your package.json with a value of 2018.  The Linter's parser fails at language features above that.  It overrides any plugins that are specifying something else.  In turn people get warnings in their tools and the PR's are checked against 2018 before review.

As far as the build tools go, the project is bundling for a brower support target not a language support target.  The syntax of the bundle is determined by this dynamic setting which changes every quarter:

```
  "browserslist": [
    "> 1%, not dead, not ie 11, not op_mini all"
  ],
```

I'm happy to  take the time to translate that back to language level (plus or minus) language features.
You have pointed out options, you can go 2020 and exclude the features you want to avoid with a few quick rules.  The parser option used above is kind of a hard upper bound that we can retreat from.

Writing this out for clarity so I can build a PR today that meets this 150 release goal:

- Developers write 2018 code without any of the bug prone language features that you want to avoid.
- Keep the `eslint-config-mdcs` plugin because it only contains style features and we can override the permissive language level specified in it's `env` config using line in the projects `package.json` as above.
- Build continues to bundle for browser target (which may contain any set of language features to meet it's goals)
- If there's anything meaningful in more recent language levels (handy import syntaxes like in the example above) , implement as 2020 stripped backwards, if not: implement as 2018 and remediate any linter issues.

How's that sound ?
I'm hoping for an ESLint configuration that warns us about use of features newer than ES2018, _except_ import/export statements which may use more recent syntax.

I need to do this in two stages.

- First is the single line to enforce 2018, and fix those 3 import statements.
- Second is relax it to 2020 parse mode, and rules to strip it back.

> I'm hoping for an ESLint configuration that warns us about use of features newer than ES2018, except import/export statements which may use more recent syntax.

After some tests by @epreston, the best way would be to achieve this result would be to use ES2020 + [eslint-plugin-escompat](https://github.com/keithamus/eslint-plugin-escompat) with the rules `no-nullish-coalescing` and `no-optional-chaining`.

I believe the other features from ES2019/ES2020 are not that relevant to this repo.
Take some more time to look into it a bit more.  There's lots of fast opinions and people don't read everything carefully.

review_comments:
Hey, exporting as plain object breaks tree-shaking, we can't have that.

Having `export * as` is fine as it gets transpiled by rollup in the build step.

That's not the case.

Let's look into that.  There are a number of objects of this style.  This new code is what the old import statement gets trans-piled to.  I have a tree-shake confirmation project published.  Will link shortly.

This is being done in 2 parts.  https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/25185

There are mutually exclusive requirements and people have some confusion.  Let's write it out.

Update: https://github.com/epreston/three-treeshake-coverage 

Please pretend you don't see the other bits.  Need an hour to cleanup my changes and commit them.

Long story short:

> Having `export * as` is fine as it gets transpiled by rollup in the build step.

Yes, it becomes something which is very similar to the new code, because that statement is shorthand for "make an object for me".  Then it gets distributed and the final bundler (client application) which does the shake.  If we want to improve the shake, we have API changes.  If we want to retain the API, distribute nearly the same bundle, and enforce 2018, we change the code.

Currently the tools are configured for 2020.  Setting the tools to 2018 and enforcing it is the first step so we actually improve the tree-shake instead of masking it.

As a confirmation take a look at what we ship now using the 2020 syntax.  I'm going to use the middle size one to reduce the reading.

The old 2020 line:

```js
export * as AnimationUtils from './animation/AnimationUtils.js';
```

Is currently being translated to:

```js
var AnimationUtils = /*#__PURE__*/Object.freeze({
	__proto__: null,
	arraySlice: arraySlice,
	convertArray: convertArray,
	flattenJSON: flattenJSON,
	getKeyframeOrder: getKeyframeOrder,
	isTypedArray: isTypedArray,
	makeClipAdditive: makeClipAdditive,
	sortedArray: sortedArray,
	subclip: subclip
});
```

This has been updated to:

```js
const AnimationUtils = {
	arraySlice: arraySlice,
	convertArray: convertArray,
	isTypedArray: isTypedArray,
	getKeyframeOrder: getKeyframeOrder,
	sortedArray: sortedArray,
	flattenJSON: flattenJSON,
	subclip: subclip,
	makeClipAdditive: makeClipAdditive
};
```

It gets translated to:

```js
const AnimationUtils = {
	arraySlice: arraySlice,
	convertArray: convertArray,
	isTypedArray: isTypedArray,
	getKeyframeOrder: getKeyframeOrder,
	sortedArray: sortedArray,
	flattenJSON: flattenJSON,
	subclip: subclip,
	makeClipAdditive: makeClipAdditive
};
```

Keeping it clean, the final bundler works its magics.  This is what I hope to demonstrate in the confirmation project.  Its possible we get slightly better tree-shake using the 2018 syntaxes.

In the old code, final bundler can only remove the whole object if its entirely unused, which will be created in any case (new or old code).  Tools can remove constants if they are entirely unused, so we have even ground.
I'm writing this all out because you are right, except if we use this particular 2020 shorthand syntax, which doesn't help the cause.

> If we want to improve the shake, we have API changes.

Actually you're correct, the object in the final bundle doesn't get tree-shaken because it's an object, and budnlers can't tree-shake that. The only way to make it tree-shakable would be to do `export * from './animation/AnimationUtils.js';`, but I'm not sure maintainers want to go with this breaking change.

> except if we use this particular 2020 shorthand syntax, which doesn't help the cause.

There is no problem with this syntax, as it doesn't end up in production. What #25185 is all about is Optional chaining and Nullish coalescing (and of course class fields from ES2022).

I guess we can enforce ES2020 and disable just Optional chaining and Nullish coalescing.

Unrelated but...

Could be nice if the CI could check if a PR makes the build bigger/smaller and also if the tree-shaked lib is bigger/smaller.
@mrdoob its on the way.  Also circular reference check.

> I guess we can enforce ES2020 and disable just Optional chaining and Nullish coalescing.

At the moment, that is not possible.  With the agreed 2018 direction, the zero impact to API and treeshake, this is the best we have.
Thanks @epreston! That would be cool. You can get the tree-shaken lib size from `test/treeshake/index.bundle.min.js`.
Also maybe it can report test coverage? I think many large projects use bots that report both build size and test coverage.
I really believe in 50% best case reduction if we make some really careful and clever moves.

> At the moment, that is not possible. With the agreed 2018 direction, the zero impact to API and treeshake, this is the best we have.

Why is it not possible?

> disable just Optional chaining

I don't think anyone wants to disable "Optional Chaining" that would drop a massive amount of code from the library and make things very robust.  Seems like half of most classes are just checking for null / undefined.



> Nullish coalescing

Yeah, that's hard to read, causes bugs, and I can't spell it correctly without looking it up.
Quick heads up, "circular reference checks" are not going to win me any friends.  Nodes has 22.  Analysis posted here: #25240 , rest of the library is clean.

> I don't think anyone wants to disable "Optional Chaining" that would drop a massive amount of code from the library and make things very robust. Seems like half of most classes are just checking for null / undefined.

We have already disabled it and all of its usages (https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/pull/25172).

> Nodes has 22. Analysis posted here: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/25240

The solution is also posted there -- I will file a PR soon.

> I don't think anyone wants to disable "Optional Chaining" that would drop a massive amount of code from the library and make things very robust. Seems like half of most classes are just checking for null / undefined.

By [Optional chaning](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Optional_chaining) I mean `?.` and currently it's only used on `GLTFExporter.js`.
Nullish coalescing is not used anywhere in three.js.

> > At the moment, that is not possible. With the agreed 2018 direction, the zero impact to API and treeshake, this is the best we have.
> 
> Why is it not possible?

Not exposed as a rule, looks like it requires a custom eslint parser to implement.
Ah yeah, well we could use the `no-nullish-coalescing` and `no-optional-chaining` rules from this plugin: https://github.com/keithamus/eslint-plugin-escompat
I see this as the best solution, because as mentioned here https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/25185#issuecomment-1422059604, the import/exports are not included in the enforcing.

That looks promising for the next step.  Thank you. 

The plan is to relax back to 2020 parsing with a set of rules to strip it back that we can turn on and off.

Can you repost that on https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/25185 so we don't lose it ?

> I see this as the best solution, because as mentioned here [#25185 (comment)](https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/25185#issuecomment-1422059604), the import/exports are not included in the enforcing.

Which solution ?  There's a few more bits to consider to enforce 2018, without setting the tools to enforce, but add extra config to "sort of" enforce 2018.  We can work towards it and we'll get there.
ES2020 + `no-nullish-coalescing` and `no-optional-chaining` would be the best solution.

The project you linked is for things that can't be polyfilled and trans-piled.  Keep in mind, Babel isn't in the toolchain.  So we don't have full polyfill and trans-pile.  Your idea has changed my mind about how much effort the next step will take.   I think it is awesome and we actually completely agree if you read what I wrote yesterday.

People keep confusing what is in the bundle vs what code is maintained.  It really is productive to have a separate discussion on the code we read and share.  Then, have another conversation about what is included in the bundle how that is presented.

At the moment, this project doesn't bundle to a language standard but a browser support standard.  The language features used look like a rough mixture of es6 which changes every quarter.  Talking about the bundle in terms of language features makes little sense when its defined in terms of browser support.

The issues I see coming up will be about perceptions, assumptions, and confusion.  The project has a standard, but it deviates from the standard, but something will fix it, then finally realising that is not what shipped.

I want to make people happy so they can produce the exact same output and remove 20 lines from the project.  If that needs to be a birds nest of tooling config, so be it.  We can make it so people can use a few 2020 features in a context of 2018.  Not keen on doing the work then having to remediate what has crept in.  Its easier to test and rationalise about with a stable base going forward.

> ES2020 + `no-nullish-coalescing` and `no-optional-chaining` would be the best solution.

That is not a complete solution or a very wise one.  We need to add to that to avoid the globals and other bits.

Would it not be better use just vars instead of `prop: var`?

```js
const MathUtils = {
	DEG2RAD,
	RAD2DEG,
	generateUUID,
	...
```

It's exactly the same thing and gets translated to the code referenced.  This style allows the internal names to be changed (many modules import one or two directly bypassing this), while ensuring the documented API is always the same.

Last bit, when it comes to Terser and minification, these interface objects reduce the bundle size.  When the public API is used exclusively, the function names themselves can be condensed into a 2 character symbol, and used that way internally.  This marks the only spot where that 2 character replacement needs to appear in its full form.
I think it's cleaner than replicating the same names all times. For this specific case, I don't see the need to use it `prop:prop` instead of `prop`, or do we have some compatibility issue here?

Minification issue, sorry, I wrote that out just as you were responding.  There's a reason many other objects in the library follow that pattern.

The alternative is if any function names change, you have to introduce this format to maintain the API, it will be created anyway if something is inline-d.  These functions are fairly common so I'm just trying to avoid creating foot-guns.

> The alternative is if any function names change, you have to introduce this format to maintain the API, it will be created anyway if something is inline-d. 

But why we would change a function name? And, if we would decide that a new name is better than the old one, we will also update the external name.

`{ prop1, prop2, ... }` format is also used in other places throught the library.

What's the goal of this feedback ?

> But why we would change a function name? 

API's and function names changing with 10 version support for old names seems to be the norm.  So much so, there's a file dedicated to it with new updates every release, `Three.legacy.js`.  

> { prop1, prop2, ... } format is also used in other places through-out the library.

I didn't write that other code.  I hope the tradeoffs and reasons were well considered.  Plenty of places where things are not as frequently imported / exported where it does not matter because it's not API.

> What's the goal of this feedback ?

Because the code style is such in files like this, for example, BufferGeometryUtils (which is external API). I think we can discuss it in another issue if it should be changed -- I suggest that you use the `{ prop1, prop2, ...` format for now.
See the reasoning above.
I still don't agree. But I think @mrdoob and @Mugen87 should decide.

You can literally add the setting, build, and see the difference.  If you're not willing to invest the 2 minutes it takes to get this outside of opinions an into facts, what can I do ? 

At each point, nobodies bothered to check before they write something.  I explain carefully.  That's as far as I can go if people wont open a text file and search for a key word.

> Last bit, when it comes to Terser and minification, these interface objects reduce the bundle size. When the public API is used exclusively, the function names themselves can be condensed into a 2 character symbol, and used that way internally. This marks the only spot where that 2 character replacement needs to appear in its full form.

Sorry, I missed that comment. So it is a trade-off between code readability and bundle size indeed... But if we plan to remove `three.min.js` this shouldn't matter very much?

Yes, the final minimized size.  

The idea of removing minified builds is crazy.  If you are importing a library into your website from a CDN, you're not shipping un-minified dependencies in production.  Seems kinda odd for people to use a CDN to improve load times but, then lose that time because the build does not have a minified distribution.

Maybe there should be a document or readme about why things are done.  I would write out use cases and purposes.  It's just fantastically odd this particular thing needs to be explained on a library project thats been around for a while.
